mcqs.question: What's the correct rule of thumb for choosing a TTL?
options: TTL should always be set to the shortest possible value regardless of the data
TTL should be as long as possible to maximize the cache hit rate
TTL should match the size in bytes of the cached value
TTL should approximate how long a wrong answer is tolerable, bounded above by how often the data actually changes
mcqs.explanation: TTL should be derived from two real numbers — staleness tolerance and change frequency — not set to an extreme in either direction. Always-shortest wastes cache-hit benefit the data could safely have given; always-longest ignores staleness risk; byte size has nothing to do with how fast the underlying data changes.

mcqs.question: Moving a key's TTL from 10 seconds to 60 seconds under the same traffic roughly does what?
options: Cuts refetch frequency about 6x, at the cost of up to 6x more worst-case staleness
Has no effect on refetch frequency, only on memory usage
Doubles the refetch frequency because jitter now has more room to apply
Eliminates staleness entirely because fewer refetches happen
mcqs.explanation: With 6x fewer expiries per unit time, the DB sees roughly 6x fewer refetches for that key — but the worst-case age of a served value also grows 6x, from up to 10s stale to up to 60s stale. It's a real trade, not a free win, and it doesn't touch memory usage or jitter's role directly.

mcqs.question: The same underlying data is shown on a preview card (tolerates a minute of staleness) and a detail page (needs to be near-live). What's the best approach?
options: Use two cache entries with two different TTLs, so each screen gets the staleness tolerance it actually needs
Use one shared TTL, picking the longer of the two tolerances
Remove caching entirely from the screen that needs fresher data
Average the two staleness tolerances into a single TTL for both screens
mcqs.explanation: Splitting into two cache entries lets the preview card keep its longer, more cache-friendly TTL while the detail page gets a much shorter one — each screen gets exactly what it needs. Sharing one TTL forces a compromise that either under-serves one screen's freshness need or wastes cache-hit benefit on the other; removing caching or averaging both give up more than necessary.

mcqs.question: A team sets a single global default TTL of 5 minutes for every cached key in the system. What's the real problem with this?
options: It wastes memory because 5 minutes is longer than necessary for every data type
It's fine as long as every cached value fits comfortably in memory
It ignores that different keys have different change frequencies and staleness tolerances, over-serving some and under-serving others
It's fine because most production systems only ever cache one type of data
mcqs.explanation: A single default can't simultaneously fit fast-changing data (where 5 minutes risks real staleness) and slow-changing data (where 5 minutes throws away refetch savings a longer TTL could have captured) — it's wrong in both directions at once, not just wasteful of memory. Memory fit isn't the issue, and real systems routinely cache many data types with different needs.
